The deal includes a youth mobility scheme, scrapping most checks on British food exports, and the linking of EU and UK emissions trading systems - see a recap here

At the CBI conference in London, First Secretary of State Louise Haigh says the deal will "bring down the cost of business [and] help with the cost of food"

This deal will matter for food exporters - but it may not have a clear visible impact at the checkout, writes economics editor Faisal Islam

The Conservatives have already said they would scrap the deal, which Kemi Badenoch has called "terrible"

Badenoch is also addressing business leaders at the CBI conference later

Burnham says the Treasury believes the new UK-EU deal could add 0.5% to the British economy over the long term, roughly equivalent to £17bn.

The PM called it the "single biggest growth measure we could take in this Parliament".

BBC Verify's Ben Chu has been taking a look at the numbers, and notes that the 0.5% estimated increase to gross domestic product does not account for growth in the population, so the expected benefit per person may be lower.

He breaks down the figures in the video below.

Shareclose panelShare pageCopy linkAbout sharingGovernment has given 'vibes' not detail - shadow foreign secretarypublished at 11:12 GMT11:12 GMT Image source, NEIL HALL/EPA-EFE/REX/ShutterstockShadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat says of the UK-EU deal that "all we're getting is vibes", since the full detail has not yet been published.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Tugendhat says it's "absolutely common sense" to improve trade relations with other countries, but says what is "absolutely extraordinary" about this deal is it "completely misses the other things" Europe is doing with other countries.

He says it asks the UK to promise to follow rules it hasn't written "in a way it doesn't ask New Zealand to do".

It's put to him that the EU-New Zealand deal still involves a lot of form filling, but in the future that may be scrapped for the UK.

"I'm not sure that's right," Tugendhat says. "Nobody has seen the treaty... what we're getting here is more vibes".

Tugendhat, who backed remain in the 2016 EU referendum, says Brexit did not fix "all of our problems" and re-joining will not do that either.

"The question is not how do we strike another deal that confuses, and distorts, and wastes time and causes distraction. But how on earth do we fix this country? And that really is about liberation of capital and about the demographics of our own people and how we get business growing here," he says.

Shareclose panelShare pageCopy linkAbout sharingHaigh says government wants conversation 'about where we might go next' on EU tiespublished at 10:46 GMT10:46 GMT Image source, UK PoolBack now to Louise Haigh, who is taking questions at the CBI conference - she is asked whether it's possible to open up the debate of rejoining the European Union without mass disruption to businesses.

Haigh says the deal agreed with Brussels on Friday marks a "fundamental reset in the relationship with the European Union", which will ease friction between the UK and the bloc.

She reiterates Burnham's position on ensuring they respect the Labour manifesto's "red lines" - those are not returning to the single market, customs union, or freedom of movement.

"Now, we'll move forward to a conversation both with the EU and with the country about where we might go next," she adds.

She's asked if under the deal agreed on Friday MPs will not be able to block any new rules coming out of the EU on food and drink standards.

Haigh says the deal means the UK will have a seat at the table in a way it doesn't currently, removing red tape and ensuring farmers who already comply with the rules don't have to pay to prove it.

Shareclose panelShare pageCopy linkAbout sharingCBI boss welcomes UK-EU deal and says Brexit was 'wrong turn' for economypublished at 10:14 GMT10:14 GMT Image source, PA MediaA little earlier we heard from the CBI's chief executive Rain Newton-Smith, who said businesses are "impatient to grow" and called on the government to "back us to deliver" for the country.

Addressing the business group's annual conference, she says it is "time we gave a shot of confidence to our economy".

She adds the UK is stuck in a "financial strait jacket" servicing debt and facing an increased tax burden.

She tells businesses: "It's you who can give the UK hope."

Newton-Smith adds that the Budget left too many questions over the economy and the government's 10-year plan and spending review must provide answers for businesses.

"Give us decision, give us detail, and give us action," she says.

Newton-Smith says the PM made "real progress in the deal on Friday", but the "journey must continue" because "Brexit was a wrong turn for our economy".

She says "this is no time to refight the referendum" but that the UK needs a closer relationship with its biggest trading partner.

Shareclose panelShare pageCopy linkAbout sharing'We have a far better deal for Britain' - Haighpublished at 10:03 GMT10:03 GMT Image source, PA MediaFirst Secretary of State Louise Haigh is now speaking at the CBI conference, where she is making the case for Burnham's new UK-EU deal.

She calls it a deal that will "bring down the cost of business, help with the cost of food" and "reduce needless red tape".

She says the EU's "Made in Europe" policy - which aims to protect European industries from unfair competition - posed "serious risks" to critical industries in the UK including the automotive and steel industries.

But Haigh now says that due to Burnham's "courage" on taking on the EU alignment debate, "we have a far better deal for Britain".

In an "uncertain world", she says, the UK "must compete harder than ever for our place".

There is cause for optimism as the economy is performing "far better than many had predicted" despite the Middle East conflict pushing up costs, she says.

Shareclose panelShare pageCopy linkAbout sharingThis cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will followpublished at 09:53 GMT09:53 GMTFaisal IslamEconomics editor

The prime minister made a lot of the UK's new deal with the EU cutting costs for business and consumers during tough times.

In another world, Andy Burnham would have loved for the nation's supermarkets to clearly announce that they could cut food prices as a result of this latest agreement on food exports.

And while grocers have very much welcomed Friday's announcement, they have notably not committed to price cuts as a direct result of this move.

The managing director of M&S, Alex Freudmann, called the deal a "major step forward", saying it would remove bureaucracy. Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy added it was "good news for British farmers and producers".

This deal will matter for food exporters - but it may not have a clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders say there are too many moving parts in the world economy, especially given the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

It is more a hope than will at this stage. The industry and government hope that the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers.

You can read my full analysis piece here.

Shareclose panelShare pageCopy linkAbout sharingBurnham to address MPs on a new UK-EU dealpublished at 09:37 GMT09:37 GMTAdam GoldsmithLive reporter

Prime Minister Andy Burnham will head to the Commons this afternoon to set out his new post-Brexit deal with the European Union and take questions - with many on the opposition benches highly sceptical.

He's expected to tell Parliament the "landmark" agreement means there is a "very real prospect" the next decade can be "much better" than the last one.

The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading, and a youth experience scheme - but we're yet to see the official document.

Consensus is yet to be reached on a deal over university tuition fees, after calls from the EU side for a reduction for their students at British universities to match UK rates - talks are expected to continue with the aim of concluding within six months.

Not everyone agrees with Burnham's decision to reignite the debate on the UK's relationship with the EU; Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair", and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".

Louise Haigh, who runs the Cabinet Office, is speaking to business leaders at the Confederation of British Industry conference in London this morning, and Badenoch is expected to use her speech there just after midday to criticise the new EU deal.

We have reporters in the room - we'll bring you updates throughout, and then from the Commons later in the day.
